title: #71 Lower the Content Demands When Introducing a New Routine
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Barton applies a cognitive-load argument, illustrated with a diagram from Peps McCrea, to the start-of-year task of introducing new classroom routines. His claim is that when a routine's structure is unfamiliar, students must devote a large share of their limited attention to learning the rules of the routine itself, leaving little capacity to think about the actual content the routine is meant to deliver -- so pairing a brand-new routine with genuinely demanding content wastes both, since neither gets sufficient attention. His fix is to deliberately strip the content down to something trivial while the routine itself is new: introducing mini-whiteboards with a favourite-food prompt rather than a quadratic equation, introducing Turn and Talk by having students share sibling names rather than debate a maths concept. Once the routine is automated and requires minimal conscious attention, Barton argues, the content demands can be ramped back up, since students' attention is now free to engage with harder material.
points: Barton's underlying claim is a cognitive-load one: unfamiliar routine structure and demanding content compete for the same limited pool of student attention, so combining both wastes both.
The fix is sequencing, not avoidance: temporarily use trivial content purely to let students automate a routine's structure before reintroducing real content.

Once a routine is automated, it requires minimal conscious attention, freeing capacity for the harder content the routine was originally meant to support -- meaning the low-content phase is an investment, not a permanent simplification.
The tip is explicitly framed as a start-of-year strategy, since the beginning of the year is when the largest number of new routines are typically introduced at once.
quotes: When routines are unfamiliar, students have to dedicate a large proportion of their limited attention to the routine's structure - in other words, the rules of the routine.
This leaves little attention to think about the content of the routine - the things you actually want them to be thinking about to help them learn.
Using an unfamiliar routine as a vehicle to ask students to think hard about tricky content will achieve little, as neither the structure nor the content will receive sufficient attention.

To develop the routine for responding on mini-whiteboards, initially ask students to write their favourite food or their name, hover and show you, instead of asking them to write the answer to a quadratic equation.
Practising with low content demands is a fast-track towards routine automation.
When the routine is familair, students only need to give minimal attention to the structure and can dedicate their remaining attention to the content.
